content:
The "72 virgins" has become a joke and a slander. It is not a Quranic number, and it is not the main thing the Quran says about Paradise.

This article sets out what the Quran says about the ḥūr ʿīn, where the number seventy-two comes from, what the Quran promises to women and to men alike, how Muslim scholars have read the Quran's pictures of Paradise, and why the claim about suicide attackers has no support in the sources. A theory about the Syriac origin of the word is also addressed.

The Quran speaks of "ḥūr ʿīn", companions with wide, lustrous eyes (44:54; 52:20; 56:22). It calls them "restraining their glances" (55:56). It gives no number.

The figure of seventy-two comes from a report in al-Tirmidhi, which Ibn Majah and Ahmad also record, listing the rewards of the martyr in the way of God. Its grading is disputed: al-Tirmidhi called it hasan sahih, Darussalam grades it hasan, some modern hadith critics accept it, and others call the chain weak.[1]

A single report with a disputed grade does not carry the weight of a doctrine. Jurists build rulings on the Quran and on well-attested reports, and a reward on which the Quran is silent, and which rests on one contested line of narration, is held at that level of certainty. Even on the report's own terms the number belongs to the martyr and not to every believer.

The Quran's pictures of Paradise include many figures besides the hur. It speaks of young servants, "immortal youths", who go round among the people of Paradise with cups, and who look like scattered pearls.[2] No reader takes these as a promise of servants in the worldly sense. Like the hur, they belong to a set of images of honour, welcome and abundance, addressed to an audience whose idea of luxury was a well-served household in a garden.

The Quran does not restrict spouses in Paradise to men. "Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, rejoicing."[3] It promises "pure spouses" to the believers (2:25; 3:15; 4:57). Scholars have said that the women of the believers will be there and that God will give each person a spouse suited to them.

Entry to Paradise is promised to men and women on equal terms. Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, and is a believer, will enter it (4:124), and in Paradise each will have whatever the soul desires (41:31; 43:71).[4]

The Quran's descriptions of the ḥūr are addressed to men, and the book does not spell out the particulars of women's reward in the same detail. The commentators noted the point and answered it by the general promise above. They differed on whether the ḥūr are a separate creation or the believing women of this world renewed, and neither view makes Paradise a place of one-sided reward.

A well-known report shows how the Prophet himself answered the question for women. An elderly woman asked him to pray that she would enter Paradise, and he told her, teasing, that no old woman would enter it. When she went away in tears, he explained that God would recreate the women of Paradise young, reciting the verses that describe them made anew.[5] The joke turned on the same verses that describe the hur, and the commentators who held that the believing women of this world are the hur of the next found support in it.

The Prophet reported that God said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined."[6] The Quran says the same: no soul knows what has been hidden for them of joy (32:17).[7] A saying reported from Ibn Abbas holds that nothing of this world is in Paradise except the names.

The Quran's pictures, of gardens, rivers, silk and companions, are taken from what people know. Faruqi, writing on how the Quran speaks of the transcendent, noted that its descriptions of God and the unseen use earthly words while denying that they apply "simpliciter", the way a pointer works, and that the proper stance is bilā kayf, accepting them without asking how.[8]

A critic will say that this is an evasion, since the descriptions are concrete. The tradition replies that the Quran sets the highest reward elsewhere: the approval of God, which it calls greater than the gardens (9:72).[9] The sensory images are real promises, and they stand below the vision of God, which the tradition places at the summit.

The Prophet described that vision in a famous report. Looking at the full moon, he told his Companions that they would see their Lord as they saw the moon, without crowding one another to see it.[10] Al-Ghazali argued at length that the vision of God is the greatest pleasure of Paradise, because the deepest desire of the soul is to know God, and that the other pleasures are lesser in proportion.[11] A reader who takes the Quran's images to be its whole account of Paradise has read the least of it.

The strongest form of the objection says that the images still reveal the values of the book: a reward described in sensual terms is a sensual reward. The tradition answers that a body raised from the dead is still a body, and that the Quran promises a renewal of the whole person, body and soul. It describes that renewal in language a human being can understand, and it says plainly that the reality exceeds the language.

The idea that a suicide attacker earns a number of virgins has no place in the sources. The Prophet said that a person who kills himself will be punished in Hell, and the Quran says "Do not kill yourselves."[12] The Quran also forbids killing the innocent, and scholars across the schools have rejected suicide attacks on civilians.[13]

The report of the seventy-two applies to the martyr, defined by the jurists as one killed in lawful fighting, and the Quran itself promises no number to martyrs. A person who sets out to kill civilians has transgressed the Quran's rule that killing one person unjustly is like killing all mankind (5:32), and has put himself outside the report's terms.

A report from the campaign of Khaybar shows how seriously the Prophet took the manner of a death. A man fought so bravely for the Muslims that the Companions praised him, and the Prophet said that he was among the people of the Fire. Some followed him to see why, and found that when he was wounded he fell on his own sword. The Prophet then said that a man may do the deeds of the people of Paradise in the eyes of others while he is of the people of the Fire.[14] Courage in battle did not cancel the sin of taking his own life.

A small number of contemporary scholars have defended attacks of this kind in particular wars. Most scholars rejected their view, and the classical books supply no precedent for it.

A theory that ḥūr means "white grapes" in Syriac is rejected by scholars of Arabic and Syriac. The word is ordinary Arabic and appears in the poetry of the pre-Islamic period, and the theory does not fit the verses' sense.

The theory comes from Christoph Luxenberg's book on the Syro-Aramaic reading of the Quran, which proposes that many obscure words are mistaken Syriac.[15] Most reviewers have rejected the method. In the verses the ḥūr are married to the believers (52:20), described by the eyes and by the restraining of the glance (55:56), and a fruit does not restrain a glance.

The reviews came from specialists in both languages. François de Blois, reviewing the book in the Journal of Qur'anic Studies, concluded that its Syriac was often mistaken and its method arbitrary, and other scholars of Aramaic and early Arabic reached similar verdicts.[16] The questions Luxenberg raised about the early written text of the Quran are discussed seriously by scholars. His particular readings of the hur have found little support.

The Arabic root points to the whiteness and blackness of the eye, which is how the classical dictionaries explain the word. The theory has the effect of removing a difficulty by changing the language, and the evidence needed to support such a change is missing.

The bottom line

The Quran names the ḥūr ʿīn and gives no number. The seventy-two comes from one report about the martyr whose grade is disputed, and a doctrine cannot rest on it. The Quran promises Paradise to men and women on equal terms, speaks of it in images that scholars read as pointers to what cannot be described, and puts the approval of God above them.

The popular picture of a reward for violence has no basis in the Quran, in the Prophet's reported teaching, or in the rulings of the schools. The sources condemn killing oneself and killing the innocent. A reader who wants to judge the doctrine can do so on the texts above, which are few and plain.

Those texts also show what the Quran wants its reader to take from Paradise. Its descriptions are an invitation to patience, honesty and mercy in this life, addressed to men and women alike, with the promise that no good deed, however small, is ever lost before God. A belief in reward that makes a person kinder and more just is the belief the Quran describes. A belief that makes a person cruel has misread every single verse it claims to follow.

Its grading is discussed by the scholars of hadith. Jami al-Tirmidhi 1663 (Book of the Virtues of Jihad), report of al-Miqdam ibn Madikarib, which sunnah.com shows al-Tirmidhi calling hasan sahih and Darussalam grading hasan; Sunan Ibn Majah 2799 (Book of Jihad), graded hasan (Darussalam), both checked on sunnah.com.

  4. Quran 4:124; 41:31; 43:71.

  6. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, a hadith qudsi. Sahih al-Bukhari 3244 (Beginning of Creation, "The characteristics of Paradise"), report of Abu Hurayra, and Sahih Muslim 2824a (Book of Paradise), checked on sunnah.com; Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 318 (Shamela text), for Bukhari 3244.

  12. Quran 4:29; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Sahih Muslim 109a (Book of Faith, "The strict prohibition of killing oneself"), report of Abu Hurayra, checked on sunnah.com.
  13. Quran 5:32; the 2005 fatwa of the Fiqh Council of North America against terrorism.
  14. Sahih al-Bukhari 2898, Book of Jihad, report of Sahl ibn Sa'd.
  15. Christoph Luxenberg, Die syro-aramäische Lesart des Koran (Berlin: Das Arabische Buch, 2000).
  16. François de Blois, review of Christoph Luxenberg, Die syro-aramäische Lesart des Koran, Journal of Qur'anic Studies 5, no. 1 (2003): 92–97.
